title: Pomegranate Compound May Improve Stiff-Heart Failure, Study Finds
excerpt: King's College London researchers found that urolithin A, made by gut bacteria after eating pomegranates, improved heart function up to 80% in animal models of stiff-heart failure by activating a key relaxation protein.
body:
• Scientists at King's College London found that urolithin A — a compound your gut bacteria produce after you eat pomegranates, walnuts, or certain berries — improved measures of heart function by up to 80% in animal models of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), a "stiff heart" condition with few effective treatments.
  • The study, published in Science Advances (Jie Su et al., 2026), identified the mechanism: urolithin A activates a protein called PKG1α at a specific amino acid (Cys 42), helping heart muscle relax. The effect was confirmed in engineered human heart tissue grown from stem cells.
  • This does NOT mean eating pomegranates will treat heart failure. No patients were involved, no clinical trial has tested it, and only some people's gut bacteria efficiently convert pomegranate into urolithin A — the study's effect came from the compound itself, not from eating the fruit.
  • If you have heart failure or its symptoms — breathlessness, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance — talk to your cardiologist about evidence-based treatments. This research points to a future drug target, not a dietary prescription.

From Pomegranate to a New Heart-Failure Target

A compound produced in the body after eating pomegranates has improved heart function by up to 80% in animal models of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) — the "stiff heart" form of heart failure that accounts for about half of all heart failure cases. The research, led by cardiovascular scientist Dr. Joseph Burgoyne at King's College London and published in the journal Science Advances, also confirmed the effect in engineered human heart tissue grown from stem cells.

The compound is urolithin A, produced when gut bacteria break down certain compounds found in pomegranates, walnuts, and some berries. Previous work had linked it to healthy ageing and mitochondrial function. The new study gives it a specific cardiac job: flipping a switch on a protein called PKG1α (protein kinase G1 alpha), which helps heart muscle relax between beats.

"In our animal model of HFpEF, urolithin A was highly effective at reducing several markers of heart dysfunction, including improving the heart's ability to relax and reducing stiffness."

— Dr. Joseph Burgoyne, King's College London

Context & Background

HFpEF is a frustrating condition. The heart can still pump normally, but it becomes stiff and cannot relax enough between beats to fill with blood — leading to breathlessness, fatigue, and reduced exercise capacity. It affects nearly half a million people in the UK alone, and its prevalence is rising as populations age and rates of obesity and diabetes climb.

It is also hard to treat. The disease is driven by many factors at once — ageing, high blood pressure, diabetes — and drugs that help a weakly pumping heart mostly fail when the problem is relaxation instead. Sildenafil, vericiguat, nitrates, and nitrites have all missed their targets in HFpEF trials. Rather than trying to raise the same biochemical signal those drugs targeted, Burgoyne's team went straight for the switch: they screened natural compounds for the ability to act on one particular sulfur atom on PKG1α — cysteine 42 — and urolithin A was the surprise winner.

In the treated animal models, the compound helped heart tissue relax, reduced fibrosis (harmful scarring), and limited the enlargement of heart muscle cells. In the lab-grown human heart tissue — grown between fixed posts so researchers could measure how it contracted and relaxed — urolithin A significantly improved tissue relaxation, giving the mechanism direct laboratory evidence in human cells.

Impact & Analysis

The significance here is a new druggable target, not a new diet recommendation. "These findings provide evidence that targeting PKG1α could be an effective new strategy for treating HFpEF," Burgoyne said, adding that "urolithin A, or drugs designed to work in a similar but potentially more potent way, could provide a basis for developing new treatments." Independent cardiologists agree on the promise and the limits: Dr. Kevin Shah of the MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute in Long Beach, California, who was not involved in the study, called it "an exciting and interesting study" that identifies a new potential treatment target — while noting that "we do need clinical studies to translate this to patients."

That caveat is doing the heavy lifting. The strongest results come from mice; the human evidence comes from tissue in a dish. There is no established dose, no safety profile in heart patients, and no reason to believe pomegranate juice replicates the experimental conditions. Urolithin A production also varies from person to person depending on gut bacteria — some people produce little of it regardless of what they eat.

Diaspora Angle

Pomegranate holds a familiar place in Indian kitchens and Ayurvedic tradition, where it has long been credited with heart-health benefits — and this study will inevitably be read as modern science confirming folk wisdom. The honest version is more nuanced: the research validates a biochemical pathway, not a traditional remedy, and it does so through a compound the body makes rather than one the fruit contains. It is a good reason to enjoy pomegranates for their real nutritional value, and a bad reason to skip prescribed heart medication.

What's Next

The road from mouse models and dish-grown tissue to a medicine is long. The researchers will need to determine whether urolithin A — or, more likely, synthetic drugs designed to activate PKG1α the same way but more potently — can safely improve HFpEF in clinical trials. For now, the study stands as an important proof of principle: stiff-heart failure has a newly identified lever, and someone has found what pushes it.
